# OrgPath × SQL Server — The Integration Bridge {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important appearance="default"}
## Status — Draft bridge between two draft anchors
Both endpoints of this bridge are pre-acceptance. The
[SQL Server Identity Transformation](index.qmd) series is **DRAFT v0.1** and its
governing decision — the **SQL Server engine-authentication decision** — is
**PROPOSED**; the [OrgPath](../orgpath-narrative/index.qmd) series is the
explanatory companion to the OrgPath substrate canon. Treat the integration
patterns here as the seam these two series share, not as accepted normative
governance, until the engine-authentication decision is accepted and both series
are reviewed against it.
:::

The two reading sequences on this portal that most often get read in isolation
are siblings. The [OrgPath](../orgpath-narrative/index.qmd) series builds a
governance substrate; the [SQL Server Identity Transformation](index.qmd) series
consumes it. Read apart, each is complete. Read together, they describe a single
movement: an Active Directory forest's organizational structure becomes a set of
Entra ID attributes, and those attributes become the access-control authority for
a SQL Server estate that no longer trusts the domain. This page names the seams
where the two meet, corrects the one place the relationship is most often
described wrongly, and proposes the order to read them in.

## The substrate and the consumer

OrgPath is the organizational coordinate system Microsoft's identity stack does
not supply on its own. The OrgPath series develops it across seventeen documents,
beginning with what the native stack provides and ending with the synthesis; the
implementation itself — populating the Entra ID attribute lineage from HR data —
is the subject of [OrgPath Book 04](../orgpath-narrative/Book_04.qmd),
"Implementing OrgTree and OrgPath." Everything downstream depends on Book 04
being done.

The SQL Server series consumes that coordinate system at exactly one structural
point: access control. [SQL Book 07](Book_07_CPT_01.qmd), "AD Group Types and the
Entra Perimeter," is where a migrated SQL Server stops being governed by AD
security groups maintained through helpdesk tickets and starts being governed by
Entra dynamic security groups whose membership is computed from OrgPath
attributes. The dependency direction is therefore fixed: the OrgPath attribute
infrastructure must precede the SQL dynamic-group access work, not the reverse.

## The five seams

| # | Seam | SQL side | OrgPath side |
|---|------|----------|--------------|
| 1 | **Dynamic-group access** | Book 07 — OU-derived groups become OrgPath dynamic groups | the dynamic-group provisioning model; the OrgPath attribute schema; the OrgPath dynamic-group definitions |
| 2 | **DBA delegation** | Book 07 Ch 2 — Administrative Unit delegation | the Administrative Unit provisioning model |
| 3 | **Migration sequencing** | Book 02 consolidation + the engine-authentication decision's consolidation gate | OrgPath Book 04 coverage maturity |
| 4 | **Conditional Access perimeter** | Book 07 — the binary outer perimeter | OrgPath-derived groups + the Conditional Access policy design |
| 5 | **Closure & drift** | the engine-authentication decision's compliance closure artifact | the OrgPath drift engine |

### Seam 1 — Dynamic-group access (the one most often described wrongly)

This is the load-bearing seam, and it is worth stating its mechanism precisely,
because it is easy to get wrong. OrgPath is **not** a single packed string stored
in one attribute. It is a multi-facet schema — the OrgPath attribute schema —
materialized across several Entra `extensionAttribute` slots — region,
department, division, clearance, account-type, and the rest — and a dynamic-group
rule is composed from **per-facet predicates**, not from a string comparison
against a whole path. The canonical rules are not hand-authored `New-MgGroup`
calls; they are **rendered** by the dynamic-group library from the OrgPath
dynamic-group definitions against the active per-facet Codebook, under the
dynamic-group provisioning model and its rendering library. SQL Book 07's worked
example — a single-facet rule that admits a principal whose OrgPath attribute
matches and whose title contains "DBA" — is an illustrative slice of that general
model, not the whole of it. Any integration artifact that hardcodes a single
`extensionAttribute` holding a `path=...` string is describing a shortcut the
substrate does not take.

### Seam 2 — DBA delegation

Once SQL access rides on Entra groups, the people who manage those groups need a
scope. [SQL Book 07 Chapter 2](Book_07_CPT_02.qmd) puts DBA-team membership
management inside an Administrative Unit so a DBA can manage the SQL groups for
their branch and nothing else. That Administrative Unit is the OrgPath-shaped
delegation surface the Administrative Unit provisioning model provisions — the
same branch structure that drives the dynamic-group rules also bounds who may
edit them.

### Seam 3 — Migration sequencing

The engine-authentication decision makes estate consolidation a **gate** in front
of engine-layer auth migration: an instance is migrated only after it is
classified retain or consolidation-target ([SQL Book 02](Book_02.qmd)). OrgPath
coverage is the second gate on the same instances. A business unit whose OrgPath
attributes are not yet populated cannot have its SQL access expressed as dynamic
groups, so migration waves follow **both** the consolidation classification
**and** OrgPath coverage maturity. The series do not assert calendar dates for
this; the decision's own plan is anchored to the program's 2027-04-01 NTLM
backstop, not to fixed quarters.

### Seam 4 — Conditional Access perimeter

Book 07 closes on the architectural dividend: once every SQL login is a type-E
login backed by an Entra principal, Conditional Access becomes a **binary** outer
perimeter — device compliance, Named Locations, sign-in risk — that a single
surviving Windows login would bypass entirely. The principals that perimeter
evaluates are the OrgPath-derived groups; the Conditional Access design that
governs them is the same one the OrgPath series develops as the cloud successor
to GPO logon restrictions ([OrgPath Book 15](../orgpath-narrative/Book_15.qmd)).
The two series describe one perimeter from two sides.

### Seam 5 — Closure and drift

The engine-authentication decision defines the per-instance compliance record as
the closure artifact for the SQL Server authentication transformation —
`LoginMode = 1`, zero type-S/W/G logins, `sa` disabled, Arc + Managed Identity
healthy, CA-MFA satisfied — and makes closure **continuously verified**, not a
point-in-time claim. That continuous posture is where the substrate's own drift
discipline — the OrgPath drift engine — closes the loop: an OrgPath drift on a
SQL-governing dynamic group is not a cosmetic event, it is a change in who can
reach the database, and it surfaces as a compliance signal for the transformation
rather than disappearing into manual group management.

## Recommended reading order

The two series interleave; reading either straight through leaves the seam
implicit. This order makes the dependency explicit.

| Step | Read | Why here |
|------|------|----------|
| 1 | OrgPath Books 01–04 | Understand the substrate and **build it** (Book 04 is the attribute-population prerequisite) |
| 2 | SQL Books 01–03 | The authentication inheritance, estate consolidation, and the discovery audit |
| 3 | SQL Books 04–06 | The Arc identity bridge, the login migration, NTLM elimination at the SQL layer |
| 4 | **SQL Book 07** ←→ OrgPath Book 04 | **The seam** — dynamic-group access and the Conditional Access perimeter consume the substrate from step 1 |
| 5 | SQL Books 08–10 | The upstream application chain, the transformed steady state, and the ADCS → Cloud PKI dependency |
| 6 | OrgPath Book 15 | The substrate synthesis as a capstone, now that you have seen a consumer end-to-end |

## What this bridge deliberately does not claim

For the avoidance of doubt, and because earlier external syntheses of this
relationship got these details wrong:

- It does **not** claim OrgPath lives in a single `extensionAttribute` as a
  packed path string. OrgPath is a per-facet schema across multiple attributes,
  and rules are composed from per-facet predicates.
- It does **not** prescribe hand-authored `New-MgGroup` commands as the way to
  create SQL access groups. The canonical groups are rendered from the OrgPath
  dynamic-group definitions against the Codebook and extended by governed change.
- It does **not** assign fixed calendar-quarter milestones to the integration.
  Sequencing is gated by consolidation classification and OrgPath coverage, with
  the program's 2027-04-01 NTLM block as the only fixed date in the plan.
